why: It shows how large the greatest farmhouses grew (the hereditary village headman's Hirayama house of 1769, 30 meters along its ridge; the district headman's Yoshimura house, over 40 meters across its front) and that some roofs now sheeted in metal were thatched first (the Takano and Nasu houses); the tiled or sheeted roofs it traces to an earlier covering were board, not thatch (the Kita and Ishiba houses). Its limits are those of any list of designated houses: they are the survivors, the large and the notable, so it says nothing of an ordinary house. Each size it gives is one dimension, not a floor area. A district headman (大庄屋), who governed a group of villages, stands a scale above a village headman. Its dates run into the Meiji era (1901, 1905, 1907), so an entry's date must be read before its form is taken as premodern. Most of the re-roofings it records are twentieth-century repairs (one is dated 1963). The Agency for Cultural Affairs' designation database gives each house's dimensions from its designation record and is the closer source for a size.

One sentence says in which districts ordinary farmhouses took the irimoya roof, which is what places it on a map. Its limits: flagged on the page itself for possible original research, and the sentence's own reference is Kon Wajirō's 1943 revision of his 1922 book on Japanese folk houses, so it describes the houses standing in the early twentieth century, many of them built or altered after the Edo period. It speaks of Japan only - mountain districts near Kyoto and in Kai, Sagami and Musashi, named as where such houses are many, not counted - and says nothing of Chinese farmhouses.

It names the three-sided house as a basic Han house form and names the simpler single-range and L-shaped forms beside it, so a Chinese-leaning village has more than one plan to draw. Its limits: a short article that Wikipedia itself has flagged since 2022 as citing no sources for its body (its three footnotes support only the Taiwanese and Hakka names), so it carries the shape of these forms and not their authority; the single-range and L-shaped forms are named in one line and not described; its examples are standing houses in Taiwan, Fujian and Bangkok of no stated date, so it shows the late-imperial southern form, not any dated era; its account of who lived in which room is the ideal, not a survey; it gives no sizes and no share of households in each form.

It says the three-sided courtyard house is found across China, not in one province, and that the showy swallowtail ridge is commonly seen on temples, mansions and ancestral halls; it does not say ordinary houses lack it, so "a mark of the rich" is our reading, not its statement. Its limits: a short article about one region's style (southern Fujian and Taiwan, as surviving buildings show it), with no figures; its "found across China" is a single passing sentence whose one footnote is a web page on Taiwan's Minnan houses, so it carries the shape of the claim, not proof of how widespread the form was.

It states the look of a south Chinese house from outside and above - white walls under dark tile - in one well-known region. Its limits: the page itself carries a neutrality warning; Huizhou was a merchant region whose showpiece villages are not typical of poor farmers; and it gives no figures. Its "white walls, black tile" line (白墙黑瓦) has no footnote, and most of its references are pages from a provincial tourism bureau and news sites, so it is good for the look and not for anything more exact.

Its description of the plant (60-130 cm tall; white, pale-red or red flowers; green to deep-red stems; harvest about 70-80 days after sowing) carries no footnote of its own. The height and the stem colors are botany and hold in any century, within the spread of variety and soil. The flower colors do not wholly: Japan's red-flowered buckwheat (Takane Ruby, registered 1993) was bred from a Himalayan landrace, so a pre-modern field in this setting is drawn white to pale pink. The 70-80 days is a modern figure for modern varieties (the article gives 60-75 days for those bred since the 1980s); a pre-modern landrace's season was short too, but the number is not a period count. Its cultivation figures describe modern Japanese farming; of pre-modern practice it says only that buckwheat was grown in slash-and-burn fields from the Yayoi period and on mountain land, nothing of how a field was sown.

Foxtail millet is one of the oldest grains of Japan and China, and the plant's height and ripening color are botany rather than practice. Its height (about 150 cm) and its months come from modern popular books on grains (Hayashi 1998, Taira 2017), and the yellow drooping ears have no citation at all. The months (sown May to June, harvested late September to October) are the general modern Japanese ones for one growing pattern. The article itself separates a spring millet for cold regions from a summer millet for warm ones, and notes millet grown between rows of wheat or after it, so a place modeled on north China may sow and harvest on a different calendar. It gives no field layout.
The second of the two millets these fields grow; the plant's height and the shape of its head are botany. It notes the cultivated forms vary widely, so its height is a range, not a figure.

It states the defensive intent behind the temple district, which is why our capital draws its temple row at the rim. The sentence quoted speaks of the time before the Edo period, which is earlier than most of what our capitals are drawn from.

It describes the look of a ripening barley field and its place in the rice year from Kanto to Kyushu, which is what a map in early summer shows. The passage we use - barley sown after the rice harvest and cut before transplanting, the pale-brown field, 麦秋 - carries no footnote of its own; its ripening dates (late May to early June) are given in the Gregorian calendar, as the crop falls now. The cropping pattern it describes is the Japanese one (China appears only as barley overtaken by wheat and rice), and its one line on when the winter crop spread - double cropping in the medieval period - cites a modern paper on barley flour, so that account is general.

It records what a soybean field looks like month by month - how tall the plants stand and when the field turns from green to yellow-brown. It describes one modern, machine-sown, lightly sprayed field of soybeans alone, about 3.5 hectares - far larger than a premodern household's plot - in Hokkaido, a cold northern region opened to Japanese farming only from the Meiji era, so it has no premodern counterpart in the setting's model and its months run late. Its one height - the top leaves near 80 cm in late August - is that of a modern variety and is carried only as a rough bound on how tall a field stands; the turn from green to yellow-brown in the weeks before harvest is what the maps take from it as it stands.

It distinguishes the pond built on flat farmland from the one dammed in a valley, which is the distinction a map draws. It describes one region's ponds as they stand today, and gives no date or era for any of them: it says only that the ponds "were made", so it carries the forms and not their age, which must come from another source. Its only figures are that a valley chain runs to three or four ponds and that one plains pond, Kako-Oike, covers 49 ha; it is an explanatory page, used for the shape of each kind and not for measurement.

It is why a chrysanthemum reads as the Emperor's flower in a setting drawn on Japan. Its sentence on Go-Toba and the Kamakura emperors cites no source of its own. It says the crest was the Emperor's by custom only. In the Edo period the design was used freely on sweets and Buddhist altar goods, and the bans on others using it are Meiji decrees of 1868-1871, later than the eras the setting is drawn on. So it supports the flower reading as the Emperor's, not the flower being reserved to him. It says nothing about growing the flower or about any planted field.

It shows a village on a city's edge given over to growing plants, chrysanthemums among them, for the city's market. A municipal page reporting the 1824 catalogue second-hand; its market was Edo, a city of about a million, and a whole village of specialist growers is evidence for the edge of a great city, not of an ordinary town; it gives no areas or plot sizes, and Somei's nurserymen grew trees and potted plants rather than field crops of flowers.

It records the scale of Edo's chrysanthemum trade on the city's edge - dozens of nurseries and a hundred stalls. It takes the figure from records it does not name, and it misdates the one period text it quotes, the Edo meisho hana-goyomi, to 1847 (Bunsei 10 is 1827). The count is the peak of one of three passing crazes in the mid-to-late Edo period, not a standing number. It is also the nursery belt of a capital of about a million people, more than a town's edge would carry. It says nothing about fields or their size.
It places the town on its river. Its 4 m moat is a measurement of the restored World Heritage site as it stands today, with no period source given for it.

It is a Chinese instance of chrysanthemums grown as a field crop for sale, which the Japanese sources lack, but the crop it describes is the present-day one (one of the "Zhejiang eight" medicinal herbs, sold nationwide), not a premodern one. Its origin story is a tradition it repeats, not a documented history: Southern Song officials settled at Tongxiang and "built gardens and planted chrysanthemums" (建园栽菊), which is gardens, not fields. The Song text it quotes (a "Zhifu quanji" 致富全集) cannot be identified as a Song work, and the passage is about flower displays at Lin'an, not Tongxiang. It gives no field sizes, and its modern output figures (1 billion yuan a year; "10,000,000 tonnes" a year, plainly an error) must not be used.

It sets one station's inns against its houses and population, which shows how much of a post town's street was inn. Kusatsu, a junction of two highways, is busier than most stations, and the page itself gives a higher inn count at another time (132 against 72). Its 1843 counts are credited to the shogunate's Tōkaidō shukuson taigaichō survey, but without a footnote. Its own line that one house in five or six was an inn has no source and does not follow from its 1843 figures, where 72 inns among 586 houses is about one in eight.

It gives the standing numbers on each class of highway and says the horses and men were requisitioned from the station's residents. Its limits are that only the Nipponica entry names the scholarship behind its figures (Kodama 1960, Maruyama 1975). The 1601 figure of 36 horses was ordered for the Tokaido's stations only. The 1638 date and the "many stations" qualification come from one of its entries only. All the numbers are for post stations on the shogunate's trunk highways (the Nakasendo's quota was briefly cut to 25 and 25 in 1661), not for towns in general. And the fixed numbers are what was ordered, which the same entries say fell short as traffic grew.

It records that even this model Chinese walled town put one side of its wall along a river. Its dimensions describe the wall as it survives after Ming rebuilds and modern conservation, not as first raised. The article lists no references at all, and another page gives its towers every 60 m rather than 50.

It says what set the waki-honjin apart from the honjin and from the inns. It is a short stub that cites no sources, so what it says rests on the encyclopedia's word alone and cannot be traced to a reference; it gives no sizes.

It is the nearest historical institution to the setting's waystation - a state relay station on a trunk road with a fixed complement of horses - and it says some stations were run by the district office. Its limits are that the horse numbers are a rule of the eighth-century statutes (the page cites them to a 2015 popular history, and the Stable and Pasture Code is the source of the station rules beside them), which the page says rose or fell with each station's terrain; that these stations served only official couriers and their attendants (travelers of court rank could stay by exception), so they stand in for a state courier post and not an inn open to travelers; and that it describes the eighth to tenth centuries, some nine centuries earlier than the Edo sources beside it.

It is a museum's gallery text summarizing excavated evidence for the relay stations of Japan's ritsuryo state (from the late seventh century, modeled on Tang China's system), about a thousand years before the Edo post towns. The page itself calls the tiled, white-walled, red-pillared buildings rare for their time and luxurious, fit to receive foreign guests: they show the showpiece stations of a major road, not what an ordinary relay station looked like. It gives no dimensions, and its "first in the country" refers to the buildings found, at two sites together.

It is a readable description of a real Chinese post station and its layout - offices, granary, horse compound and official lodging court inside a wall. Its limits are that another page of the same site gives a different perimeter and area; that its placement of the lodging court is inconsistent within the page; that its own figures disagree, since a 2,330 m perimeter around a roughly square wall would enclose about 0.34 km², not the 0.2 km² it gives; that its garrison of more than 300 and its 82 horses are the Qing peak ("at most"), quoted secondhand from an unnamed edition of the county gazetteer; and that Jimingyi was a fortified frontier station with a garrison, far larger than an ordinary relay.
It supplies the vocabulary and the practices our moats are drawn with - the natural moat, the sectioned moat, the town moat.

It gives both a length and a breadth for a surviving road town beside its house count, the one pairing that lets a density per acre be worked out. It is one mountain station, a long thin town hemmed in by its valley, and its extent is the preserved townscape of today rather than a surveyed Edo boundary. The article takes that length and breadth from the Nagano prefectural tourism site, round figures and not a survey. It gives the 1843 counts from the shogunate's Nakasendo station survey (Nakasendo Shukuson Daigaichō) without a footnote. So a density worked from them sets an 1843 house count against an approximate present-day extent, whose 200 m breadth likely takes in hillside and temple ground beyond the house lots. It is a gross figure, not a density of the built street.

It is a signed encyclopedia statement of the contrast this record's walled-or-open knob turns on, Japanese against Chinese. It generalizes over medieval and early-modern Japan and does not treat the moated exceptions.
It states the groundwater case in plain terms, the source our inner moat is written to hold.

It names the specific Japanese towns that were enclosed and what enclosed them, which gives this record's rare moat-and-bank form its cases. It is flagged by Wikipedia since September 2015 as lacking sources, and its passage naming the moated towns (Hakata, Sakai, Hirano, Imai, the temple towns) carries no footnote, so it gives the cases' names and not evidence for them; its Japanese section is a survey of exceptions, so it says little about how common enclosure was.

It is the one readable account found of a Chinese relay town's plan, with figures, which gives the Chinese side of the post-town question a measured example. Jimingyi is a single station, singled out as the largest of its kind, on an important route near the capital, so it shows what a relay town could be rather than what an ordinary one was. Jimingyi stood on the Ming northern frontier, on the road to the Xuanfu garrison near the Great Wall, and was fortified as part of that frontier's defences: its tall wall is evidence of what the frontier required, not that relay towns in the interior were walled. Its figures are modern measurements of the surviving and partly restored Ming and Qing town, rounded ("about 2000 metres") and given without a source.

The rural town is a Japanese market town below the castle town, and the article describes its plan in words. Its standing in for a county seat is this project's analogy, not the article's: the rural town was legally a village and mostly a center of trade rather than of government (a few, such as Kurashiki and Hirano, held an intendant's or a lord's office), where the Chinese county seat was a magistrate's walled seat. It is an encyclopedia article (marked a stub) resting on cited Japanese reference works. Its plan sentence rests on a modern national town-planning guide rather than a history and speaks of most cases, not all; its planned, moated exceptions are temple-precinct towns and medieval cities, mostly in the Kinai. Its town "every few kilometers" is a loose phrase, not a measured spacing, taken from Wakita Osamu's entry in a Heibonsha encyclopedia. It describes Settsu and Kawachi near Osaka and Hirano in the late seventeenth century, the cotton-growing core of what the article calls Japan's most economically advanced region: a dense case, not a typical one. The article says such towns formed elsewhere later, around 1690-1730.

It is a field count of what grows around working farmhouses in four regions, which is what says which trees were common in a farmstead's grounds. Chestnut is among the three commonest only in the two north-eastern districts (Isawa, Iide), and persimmon only in Tonami. In warm Hikawa neither is, and cedar leads in the other three. The abstract gives the groves' purposes as shelter from wind and weather, fuel and building timber, and does not say the chestnut or persimmon were kept for their fruit. All four are districts of dispersed farmsteads, where such groves are largest, so a nucleated village's house plots need not match. Its samples are very small (four to ten homesteads a district); and it is an abstract, so only its headline figures can be read.

It lists the sources a moat's water actually came from, from a specialist rather than a guidebook, which is what our capital's moat-filling rule is drawn from. Its limit is that it ranks none of the sources.

It records the folk belief that a loquat planted in a garden or a homestead brings unending sickness, which bears on whether a farmstead kept one. It carries the belief only through two footnotes, both 20th-century Japanese folklore records: an article in the folklore journal Kyōdo Kenkyū (1916) and the Miyagi prefectural history's folklore volume (1956). The Miyagi one is from a cold northern prefecture near the edge of the loquat's range. Neither shows the belief in the Edo period, and nothing here gives a Chinese counterpart. It does not say how widely the belief was followed. The same article says Edo-period temples kept many loquats for leaf medicine and that garden loquats are common south of Chiba. So it shows only that the belief was recorded, not that farmsteads went without the tree.
It is the readable statement of the one plain case of a castle moat filled from the sea, which this page uses to show how wide the range of moat sources ran.

It confirms the pairing and the tree for the Edo period, the setting's own model, from standard dictionaries. The entries differ in how firmly they put it: one says "as a rule", others "mostly". Five of them name pine alongside the enoki, and one adds cedar, so the enoki is the usual tree but not the only one. The mounds were distance markers the shogunate set on the main highways, one pair per ri. The source bears on a place that sits on such a road, not on a village or town entrance as such.

It is the one readable page that sets out the drying methods side by side with their regions, which is what turns "the drying rack" into a choice among several forms, and it says where a rack stood and how long it could run. Its regions and rack sizes are the twentieth-century pattern from before combines replaced the rack; it says nothing of China, which the setting also draws on. Its only dates are that ground drying and stacking were in use by the Nara period (eighth century) and that a record of 841 urged rack drying, so no form's regional spread can be dated earlier than the twentieth century. Its twenty to thirty days of drying is reported as what is said, not measured, and it gives no count of racks per household.

It is where the record finds, in general-reference form, that a farm plot was usually enclosed and by what, and that the enclosure changed from east to west - the grove in the east, the outbuildings themselves farther west. The east-to-west change comes from one entry, Takeuchi's in Nipponica, which describes farmsteads as modern fieldwork found them and gives no era; only the Heibonsha entry's Edo passages rest on period survey manuals and registers. Its only figures are plot sizes (a medieval peasant's plot mostly of one to two tan, a lord's often over one chō), not counts. The Britannica entry names hedged, walled and moated plots together without saying whose was whose, and no entry says how common each enclosure was - the western one is given only as a tendency.

It states plainly that the traditional Okinawan house was generally walled in coral and limestone against the typhoons, which is one attested form of a farmstead boundary; the screening and the line between settlement and plot it gives to the hinpun, not to the wall. It gives no date for the form, and it describes the Ryukyu islands, whose climate and history differ from the Japanese main islands, so it supports the stone-walled plot only for a warm, storm-exposed, stony coast.

It dates the best-known row of drying trees along a farm road to a land consolidation of the 1940s, when the farmers moved their trees there, so this straight farm road, and the row along it, are an arrangement of the 1940s. It says only that the trees were brought "from various places" in the district, not how they had stood there. So it dates this row, but it cannot show how drying trees stood before the consolidation or in our setting. And the row survives because the district was kept for air-dried seed rice after machine drying ended drying trees elsewhere, so it is a preserved exception, not a typical landscape.
